title: If Someone Calls Your Name Three Times at Night, Don't Answer #shorts
description_hook: Korean and Chinese grandparents have one rule about voices in the dark.

lines.say: Rule one. If someone calls your name in the dark, don't answer.
lines.img: a teenage boy frozen in a dark apartment hallway at night, looking back over his shoulder at an open doorway into pure darkness, cold blue moonlight

lines.say: Rule two. Wait. A real person will call again. They say a spirit only calls twice.
lines.img: close-up of a phone screen glowing on a bedside table at night, the room behind it black, a faint silhouette standing in the doorway

lines.say: Rule three. In Korea, the reapers come in threes, and they carry a list of names.
lines.img: three tall figures in long black coats and wide black hats standing in a rainy city street at night, faces hidden in shadow, neon reflections

lines.say: Rule four. At a Korean funeral, families leave three bowls of rice by the gate. It's for them.
lines.img: three small bowls of white rice, straw sandals and coins on a low tray outside a wooden gate at night, candlelight, mist

lines.say: Rule five. If the third call comes in your mother's voice…
lines.img: a dark bedroom door slightly open, warm light behind it, a hand gripping the door frame from the other side

lines.say: …remember your mother is asleep in the next room.
lines.img: a middle-aged woman sleeping peacefully in a dim bedroom, while behind the half-open door the hallway is completely black

loop_back: The last line ends on the third call — which sends the viewer straight back to rule one: don't answer.

gumi.say: So. Would you answer? Tell me in the comments.

source: A widespread Korean and Chinese folk belief that spirits and reapers (jeoseung saja) call the living by name at night; at traditional Korean funerals families set out saja-bap — rice, straw sandals and coins — for the reapers.
